title: Berkshire Owns Both Chevron and Occidental. Which Oil Stock Is the Better Buy Now? - The Motley Fool
content: Oil prices are high, which is a relatively greater benefit to Occidental, but what happens when commodity prices fall? The global energy market has been upended by the geopolitical conflict in the Middle East, sending oil prices sharply higher. Occidental Petroleum (OXY +2.67%) appears better positioned to benefit from high oil prices than Chevron (CVX +2.88%). But don't pull the trigger just yet. There's a very important reason you may want to own Chevron instead, and it may help explain why Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA -0.84%)(BRKB -0.87%) owns both. Warren Buffett once described investing as a baseball game where nobody is calling balls and strikes. The point of that folksy example is to highlight that investors don't have to swing at every pitch; they can just wait for the pitches they like. And that's exactly how Buffett handled Berkshire Hathaway's portfolio, cherry-picking the stocks he wanted inside of it. It isn't an accident that Buffett bought Occidental Petroleum and Chevron. It was a conscious decision. And it is important to understand that they are not interchangeable energy investments. There is a notable difference between their business models. Occidental, which most investors just call Oxy, has been focused on growing its production profile. Buffett helped that process along when he assisted Oxy in buying Anadarko Petroleum. In fact, Oxy beat out Chevron for that deal. More recently, Berkshire Hathaway bought Oxy's chemicals business. Berkshire and Oxy have a long history, but the second deal highlights a clear focus on energy production. That's good right now with oil prices at lofty levels. For investors looking to capitalize on high energy prices, Oxy could be a better choice than Chevron. For now. The problem with that story is that oil prices have a long history of being volatile. They rise and fall in often dramatic fashion, driven by factors such as supply and demand, natural and man-made disasters, and geopolitical conflicts. When the event that's driving oil prices higher eventually passes, prices usually fall. When that eventually happens again, as it has every time before, Occidental will be more exposed to the downturn than Chevron. When the Total Conviction signal flashed for Nvidia in 2009, most people ignored it. The ones who acted turned $5,000 into $3,105,454*. Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. Chevron is one of the world's largest energy companies. It is what is known as an integrated company because it intentionally has exposure across the entire energy value chain, from the upstream (production) through the midstream (pipelines) and all the way to the downstream (chemicals and refining). That diversification helps to soften the impact of oil price swings. Chevron's dividend, which has been increased annually for 38 years, is the best example of how resilient its business model is. Notably, the debt Oxy took on to buy Anadarko forced it to cut its dividend in 2020 when oil prices plunged during the coronavirus pandemic. That event highlights the more aggressive approach that Oxy is taking with its business. While Oxy's leverage has fallen dramatically since then, Chevron's 0.2x debt-to-equity ratio remains below Oxy's 0.35x. So, even from a balance sheet perspective, Chevron is better positioned to deal with adversity than Oxy. If you are looking for an energy stock you can comfortably hold for the long term, even during oil downturns, Chevron may be a better choice. Oxy's dividend yield is roughly 1.8% as of this writing, while Chevron's is 3.1%. If you are looking for income, Chevron wins that comparison. But it also wins in dividend consistency, given its impressive dividend track record. While Occidental Petroleum may be better positioned to benefit from rising energy prices, it is highly likely that Buffett bought both companies as a hedge against a fall in oil prices. If you have to pick between them, Chevron's diversified and resilient integrated business model will likely be the better buy-and-hold option. In the span of a few weeks, the oil major has outlined plans to export its Texas shale playbook to Argentina, entered early talks to run a giant Iraqi oil field, and weighed parting with mature offshore assets in the Gulf of Mexico. A heavyweight in the S&P 500, Chevron jumped during the latest session and now trades above the average price objective set by rating firms. Chevron is an integrated energy company that explores for, develops, produces, transports, and markets crude oil and natural gas. Its upstream business finds and pumps hydrocarbons from fields around the world, while its downstream operations refine crude into fuels and manufacture lubricants, petrochemicals, and fuel additives. That integration gives Chevron balance across the energy cycle, since refining margins sometimes improve when crude prices fall. The company also funds lower-carbon businesses, including renewable fuels, carbon capture and storage, and hydrogen. With operations spanning several continents, Chevron is one of the largest and most closely watched energy sector companies in the world. Chevron's latest advance stood out for a company of its size and steadiness. Shares climbed sharply and finished near their intraday high, though trading activity ran somewhat below a typical day. The stock now sits well above both its short-term and long-term moving averages, with the short-term average itself well above the long-term one, the hallmark of a sustained uptrend. That momentum is notable because Chevron's beta is low, meaning it usually moves far less than the broader market. When a stock this steady moves this much, it typically reflects a genuine shift in how the market views its prospects. Chevron's share price has now climbed above the average price objective across rating firms, a sign that the rally has outpaced older forecasts. Fresh revisions are catching up. One firm raised its price objective meaningfully, while another increased its full-year earnings forecast. Models that track estimate changes suggest conditions favor another earnings beat when Chevron next reports, with year-over-year growth expected. The consensus leans moderately favorable, with one top-tier rating, a large majority of positive views, a handful of neutral stances, and a single bearish rating. Even so, the average objective has not yet caught up with the stock. Chevron's most recent quarter delivered a dramatic outperformance.  Earnings per share beat consensus estimates by a wide margin and more than tripled compared with the same quarter last year. Revenue also topped forecasts and jumped by more than half year over year, a striking increase that partly reflects a larger asset base following a major acquisition, alongside firmer energy prices. Return on equity and net margin both sit at moderate levels. Full-year forecasts call for strong earnings, and the coming release will show whether that momentum carried into the latest quarter. Chevron plans to apply the operating model it refined in the Permian Basin of West Texas and New Mexico to Argentina's Vaca Muerta shale region, backed by a large-scale, multiyear spending plan. In the Permian, Chevron learned to drill longer wells, standardize development, and squeeze more oil from each acre through better recovery techniques. Vaca Muerta is one of the largest shale formations outside North America but remains less developed. If Chevron can replicate its Permian efficiency there, the region could become a meaningful source of long-term production growth, diversifying its shale exposure beyond the United States. Chevron is reportedly considering divesting a package of mature assets in the U.S. Gulf of Mexico. Older offshore fields often require rising maintenance spending while producing less oil over time, making them better suited to smaller operators that specialize in squeezing value from aging infrastructure. Proceeds could be redirected toward newer deepwater projects and other higher-growth opportunities. That approach reflects disciplined capital allocation: shedding assets with declining returns to fund those with stronger long-term prospects. It also shows Chevron reshaping its portfolio rather than simply adding to it. Chevron has long been one of the most reliable dividend payers in the energy sector, maintaining its payout through multiple oil price downturns. The annualized  dividend yield sits at a solid level, though it has narrowed somewhat as the share price climbed. The payout ratio is moderately high, absorbing a meaningful share of earnings, which leaves less cushion if oil prices fall sharply. Chevron's strong balance sheet and integrated business help support the dividend through downturns, but its growth will ultimately depend on sustained earnings from both existing operations and new projects. Recent rating activity shows forecasters catching up at different speeds. One firm upgraded Chevron to a moderately favorable view, another reaffirmed a favorable rating with a solid objective, and a third raised its objective alongside an outperform rating. Not every move was positive. One firm trimmed its objective while keeping an outperform stance, and another cut its objective while maintaining an equal weight view. That mix explains why the average objective trails the share price. Unless more firms raise their numbers after the upcoming results, Chevron will continue trading ahead of its consensus outlook. Brent crude prices touched nearly $110 a barrel on Monday as tensions in the Middle East continued to ratchet up. A series of recent escalations, including attacks on commercial ships near the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, and Ukraine’s strike on a Russian refinery, stoked fears about a further constraint in fuel supplies, sending prices higher. Worries continued despite the U.S. government’s efforts to curtail rising prices, including planned fuel releases and changes to U.S. sanctions on Russian imported fuel. Since the U.S.-Iran war began in February, energy prices have been climbing steadily, boosting energy companies. As per Koyfin data, energy stocks have outperformed the S&P 500 by a significant margin in 2026. Exxon Mobil, Chevron, and Marathon Petroleum shares surged to 52-week highs on Monday before closing lower amid the steep climb in oil prices. XOM stock hit an annual high of $179.30 during trading hours on Monday before closing about 0.4% down. CVX stock surged to a 52-week high of $225.67, but ended the session 0.28% lower. MPC stock rallied to a 52-week high of $493.98 during regular trading, but finished the day nearly 1% down. Retail sentiment around XOM, CVX and MPC stocks was ‘bullish’ at the time of writing on Stocktwits. Retail investors in Sellas Life Sciences (SLS) are floating multibillion-dollar buyout scenarios and steep share-price gains after CEO Angelos Stergiou marked the company’s 15th anniversary with a post about its “next chapter.” SLS stock jumped 5% on Monday to $10.49, snapping three straight losing sessions. In his LinkedIn post, Stergiou reflected on Sellas’ growth from a private startup into a public biotech advancing investigational cancer treatments GPS and SLS009. “Reaching 15 years isn't just about celebrating our history; it is about stepping into our next chapter with even greater focus, drive, and resolve,” he said. He acknowledged past setbacks and thanked shareholders, employees and trial participants, while reaffirming the company’s commitment to patients. “Our mission remains deeply personal, and our promise to the patients we aim to serve is steadfast. We look forward, God willing, to the best chapters that are still to be written with GPS and SLS009,” he added. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for SLS slipped to ‘bearish’ from ‘bullish’ levels a day ago amid a 258% jump in 24-hour message volumes. One user said: “My opinion, Dr. Stergiou’s message was a master-class at reassuring EVERYONE that all is well.” A user also floated a minimum $40 billion valuation. Another user argued for a $50 billion valuation, calling a $247-per-share figure. A separate user proposed a $120 billion buyout scenario and also predicted a share price of $540-plus. Across bullish share-price predictions, including scenarios tied to clinical results, targets ranged from $100 to over $540. Discussing buyout news in case of favorable data, one user said: “If BO news post good data then there’s no stopping this beast (really no explanation required as it could go full berserker mode).” BO means buyout. Another user challenged the lofty valuations and said: “I will be so glad to get out of this ticker when it hits $15 again.” The CEO’s message comes as investors have been searching for potential deal signals in recent months. In June, a filing disclosed changes to executive severance arrangements, including lump-sum payment provisions for Stergiou. For CFO John Burns and chief development officer Dragan Cicic, qualifying departures within one month before or one year after a change of control would trigger 15 months of salary, the annual target bonus, up to 18 months of health-coverage reimbursements and full vesting of unvested equity. Sellas’ conference plans have provided another talking point. The company is listed at Booth 138, with a 20-by-30-foot space, for the Dec.12- Dec.15 American Society of Hematology (ASH) meeting in New Orleans. Major exhibitors include Eli Lilly, Pfizer, Merck, AbbVie and Bristol Myers Squibb. The booth size has fueled speculation about a partnership or acquisition. Currently, investors are awaiting data from Sellas’ two lead programs. The Phase 3 Regal trial is testing GPS, an immunotherapy targeting WT1, in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients who achieved a second complete remission following salvage treatment. Its final-analysis process is triggered by 80 deaths. Sellas reported 78 events as of May 11. Reaching 80 precedes database lock, data review and analysis before results are disclosed. The company also expects fourth-quarter topline data from its 80-patient Phase 2 SLS009 study in newly diagnosed AML, including patients with early resistance to azacitidine and venetoclax. SLS009 is also being explored in pancreatic cancer. Preclinical findings from last month showed 17.9% apoptosis (programmed cell death) in a patient-derived tumor model resistant to Daraxonrasib, versus 2.8% with Daraxonrasib alone. As of 11:13 p.m. EDT, Dow futures were up about 0.25%, while the S&P 500 futures gained 0.21% and the Nasdaq-100 futures climbed 0.15%. On Monday, the three benchmark indexes closed mixed. The Nasdaq Composite led the climb, adding more than 290 points to close 1.11% higher. The S&P 500 climbed 0.41% at close, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.07%. Technology and AI stocks were top of mind for markets on Monday as the sector reversed last week's steep selloff. Chip stocks led the climb on Monday. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) closed up nearly 2%, while the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) closed up 1.61%. Nvidia Corp. (NVDA), Micron Technology Inc. (MU) and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD) all ended the session in green. The run comes ahead of vital Q3 results that will follow this week, which are likely to set the tone for the trajectory of technology shares. “Tech earnings are key this week. Fundamentals are unchanged, but given fragile price action, we turn neutral [on] risk assets and stay neutral duration,” Ajay Rajadhyaksha, global chairman of research at Barclays, said in a note, according to CNBC. Katie Stockton, founder of Fairlead Strategies, reportedly said in a note on Monday that the week will be crucial for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, which need to hold support, while noting that a hold is possible amid widespread, short-term oversold conditions. Meta Platforms (META) and Tesla (TSLA) are due to report Q3 results later this week, while multiple other semiconductor and technology companies, including Lam Research (LRCX) and Texas Instruments (TXN), will also post their results. AI-related power companies Bloom Energy (BE) and Valero Energy (VLO), along with big entertainment companies including Netflix Inc. (NFLX), will also announce their quarterly results. Meanwhile, rising oil prices amid growing geopolitical uncertainty have put downward pressure on markets. Brent crude futures expiring in December were trading at $109.88 a barrel, up about 0.3%, while WTI crude futures expiring in November traded at $103.64 per barrel. Economist Peter Schiff said in a post on X, “Oil rose another 2.5% today. It's almost $104. If you think gas prices are high now, just wait until after the midterms when Trump has to turn off the spigots from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to keep it from running dry. Oil could hit $150, sending gas prices to record highs.” Trump Media & Technology Group Corp. (DJT): Shares of the president’s media company were in focus late Monday after the stock slipped 8%, its worst single-day drop since February, as President Donald Trump’s approval rating hit a record low. Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN): The company’s stock surged nearly 5% at close on Monday and continued to climb higher overnight after Morgan Stanley raised its price target and named it a ‘Top Pick.’ Cerebras Systems Inc. (CBRS): The AI hardware and supercomputing company was on the retail radar after shares slipped more than 5% on Monday, extending a broader selloff in the sector from last week. CoreWeave Inc. (CRWV): Shares of the neocloud company fell more than 1% in overnight trading late Monday, putting it on track for a third week of declines amid a selloff in software names. Among ETFs tracking benchmark indexes, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) all climbed overnight. Meanwhile, U.S. long-dated Treasury yields continued above 5%. At the time of writing, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield was 5.138%, and the 30-year Treasury yield was 5.473%. The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) was up 0.09% amid ‘bullish’ sentiment. Asian markets opened lower on Tuesday, with South Korea's KOSPI, Japan’s Nikkei 225, China’s SSE Composite and Australian stocks all trading lower at the time of writing. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. Shares of Broadcom, Inc. (AVGO) reversed overnight losses to edge up 0.3% late Monday as a 10-year cloud agreement with NTT Docomo did little to ease retail skepticism, with traders seeking a recovery catalyst after CEO Hock Tan’s AI “casino” remarks. AVGO stock rose nearly 2% on Monday to close at $334.59, snapping three straight sessions of losses. Broadcom extended its 2019 deal with Docomo, in which the companies will align their long-term tech roadmaps to advance the private cloud underpinning the Japanese telecom operator’s digital services. The company called it Broadcom Japan’s first “comprehensive” 10-year agreement covering VMware software licenses, technical assistance and maintenance support. Financial terms were not disclosed. VMware Cloud Foundation will be at the core of the infrastructure. The deal targets three priorities: keeping services available during system upgrades, strengthening security and resilience, and accelerating the delivery of new services. Docomo will use the platform to expand capacity and manage traffic spikes, improve security patching and anomaly detection, and run virtual machines and containers on a common platform. Automation across development, testing and releases will help shorten the time needed to introduce new features. The companies also plan to expand AI-driven operations and prepare the infrastructure for future developments, including 6G and IOWN. The agreement comes a week after Tan’s comments at a Singapore panel, where he called capital the biggest constraint on further AI development as Broadcom works through wafer and memory shortages. “A lot of investors have no clue what they're investing in, but set very extreme expectations, only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino gambling,” Tan said when asked about cheaper AI models, Reuters noted. His remarks addressed investment into the broader AI sector. Tan also acknowledged that Anthropic and OpenAI had shown an ability to generate significant revenue from their latest models deployed for AI personal assistants. SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk also subsequently responded, saying, “No crying in the casino,” weighing in on Tan’s concerns about speculative AI investments. CoreWeave reported $35.6 billion in total debt as of June 30, while its second-quarter net interest expense rose to $640 million from $267 million a year earlier. Research and advisory firm Gartner recently said in a report that artificial intelligence infrastructure investments are in danger as concerns over bloated AI capex mount. The firm said that as the commercial duopoly for primary frontier models consolidates around Anthropic and OpenAI, the cash flows to meet that massive computing asset base from neoclouds are not scaling proportionally with upfront costs. Meanwhile, major Wall Street analysts are also taking opposing stances on CoreWeave. MoffettNathanson and BNP Paribas lowered their price targets on CoreWeave, while Goldman Sachs took a more positive outlook. MoffettNathanson slashed CRWV stock’s target to $89 from $107 and kept a ‘Neutral’ rating on the shares, citing its “staggering financial obligations.” BNP Paribas also cut its price target on CoreWeave to $117 from $169 and maintained an ‘Outperform’ rating, according to The Fly. The firm said that it sees a continued deterioration in investor confidence amid its debt obligations. While higher financing costs could contain the company's ability to fund future growth, the shares are "seemingly discounting some liquidity concerns," the analyst reportedly said in a research note. However, Goldman Sachs upgraded the stock to ‘Buy’ from ‘Neutral’ and set a price target of $106, implying upside of more than 73% from its last close. The firm said ongoing volatility in the credit market raises questions about whether CoreWeave can finance its next phase of growth, and at what pace. However, Goldman also said the ongoing debate over demand for frontier vs. off-frontier intelligence, and CoreWeave's annual recurring revenue per megawatt and unlevered internal rate of return, are "biased to the upside" over the next 24 months because of tight supply. The analyst also said that CoreWeave is differentiated from other neoclouds. Chevron (NYSE:CVX) has entered a preliminary agreement with Iraq's Oil Ministry for exclusive talks to operate the West Qurna 2 field. The deal would see Chevron take over operatorship from Russia's Lukoil at West Qurna 2, one of Iraq's supergiant oil fields. Iraqi officials have outlined an opportunity to double output at West Qurna 2 as part of the prospective Chevron operated development plan.
